heading: India's crossroads in stone
body: Madhya Pradesh sits at the geographic center of India, and its history reads that way too — as a record of whoever controlled the routes running through it, from the earliest Buddhist emperors to the last Mughal-era Rajput houses. The oldest surviving chapter is Buddhist: the Great Stupa at Sanchi, one of the oldest stone structures in India, was commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE and then added to for centuries afterward, with the Satavahana dynasty responsible for the intricately carved gateways, or toranas, that still ring the site. Sanchi was never a capital or a pilgrimage town tied to a single ruler; it endured because Buddhist patronage kept renewing it long after the empire that founded it was gone.

A very different, later chapter is Khajuraho, built between roughly 950 and 1050 CE by the Chandela dynasty, who raised around 85 temples of which local tradition and most popular accounts say only 22 survive today — though the Archaeological Survey of India's own page instead gives 25 standing temples; this page does not resolve the discrepancy. The temples are known worldwide for their sculpture, including the explicit erotic carvings that have made Khajuraho a subject of persistent, unresolved scholarly debate — theories range from tantric ritual symbolism to a straightforward celebration of life stages, and no single explanation commands consensus.

The state's Mughal and Rajput-era history is written in its forts rather than its temples: Gwalior Fort, which the Mughal emperor Babur himself called "the pearl amongst fortresses in India," and the Orchha fort complex, built by successive Bundela maharajas and showing the same fusion of Rajput and Mughal architectural habits found across north-central India. Together with the prehistoric rock shelters at Bhimbetka, these give Madhya Pradesh three UNESCO World Heritage sites spanning from the Stone Age to the medieval period — a range no single dynasty's story could cover.
The places on the map below move through that same span: Ashoka's Buddhist stupa, the Chandela temple city, and the forts that mark the region's later centuries as a contested Rajput-Mughal frontier.
